job.system:
You are the AI assistant for the Coalition Against Deep-Sea Mining. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: The Coalition Against Deep-Sea Mining (CADM) is a nonprofit advocacy organization based in Washington, DC. We believe that the industrial mining of the deep seabed, meaning the large-scale extraction of minerals from the ocean floor, poses a serious risk of irreversible destruction to deep-ocean ecosystems, and that no one currently knows how to conduct it without such damage. Our goal is a legally binding prohibition on commercial deep-sea mining, first in the United States and then through an international treaty. We work through lobbying, grassroots organizing, and public education.

Current focus: Our top priority this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act, which we strongly support. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup, can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
# S. 2817 Issues Review (Manager's Amendment of Oct. 6)

Below are the issues I found, numbered and grouped by section. The ones I'd raise first at markup are marked **[Priority]**.

## Sec. 2: Definitions

1. **[Priority] Sec. 2(1)(A), "by a single vessel."** The 10,000-ton threshold applies per vessel. An operator could spread recovery across two or more vessels, each under 10,000 tons, and mine unlimited total tonnage legally.

2. **[Priority] Sec. 2(1)(A), the 10,000-ton threshold.** Any operation under 10,000 tons per year per vessel is not "commercial deep seabed mining," so pilot or early-stage commercial operations are fully legal. The threshold also gives no protection against the seabed damage done by smaller operations.

3. **Sec. 2(1)(A), "per year."** The bill doesn't say whether this means a calendar year, a fiscal year, or any rolling 12-month period. That creates timing games and makes it unclear on which day a violation begins.

4. **Sec. 2(1)(A), "recovery."** The definition covers only minerals actually recovered. It may not reach collector-vehicle trials, nodules gathered and left on the seabed or discarded, or other seabed disturbance, even though that disturbance is the main source of ecological harm.

5. **Sec. 2(1)(A), "vessel."** Recovery using a fixed platform, a moored structure, or autonomous seabed equipment that isn't a "vessel" arguably falls outside the definition.

6. **Sec. 2(1)(A), "other mineral resources," "seabed," and "depths greater than 200 meters."** None of these is defined. "Mineral resources" could be read to cover oil, gas, or sand and gravel, which would invite opposition and overbreadth challenges. The bill also doesn't say how depth is measured or whether subsurface resources count.

7. **[Priority] Sec. 2(1)(B), "the Secretary."** "Secretary" is never defined anywhere in the bill (Commerce? Interior?), so this clause has no clear implementing official.

8. **[Priority] Sec. 2(1)(B), the open-ended Secretary determination.** Criminal liability under Sec. 5(b) can turn on an agency determination made with no standards, procedure, notice, or comment. That invites void-for-vagueness, due process, and nondelegation challenges. It also leaves coverage up to whichever administration holds office, and a hostile Secretary could simply decline to make any determinations.

9. **[Priority] Sec. 2(2), "U.S. person."** Only citizens and corporations organized under State law qualify. That leaves out:
   - LLCs, partnerships, and trusts (arguably not "corporations")
   - federally chartered entities
   - permanent residents and U.S. nationals
   - possibly entities organized in D.C. or the territories, since "State" is undefined
   - foreign subsidiaries of U.S. companies, which could carry out the mining offshore

10. **Sec. 2(3), "covered vessel."** The 5,000 gross-ton floor exempts smaller vessels from the registry. "Equipped for the recovery" is vague. The definition also doesn't match Sec. 2(1)(A), which uses "vessel," not "covered vessel," so a vessel can mine without ever being subject to registration.

## Sec. 3: Prohibition

11. **[Priority] Sec. 3(a), "in the United States."** The bill doesn't say whether this includes the territorial sea, the EEZ, or the outer continental shelf. A foreign company mining in the U.S. EEZ could argue it is not "in the United States" and is not a "U.S. person."

12. **[Priority] Sec. 3(a), what is prohibited.** The bill bans only "engag[ing] in" mining. It does not ban:
   - financing, sponsoring, insuring, or chartering vessels for mining
   - processing in the U.S.
   - importing or buying deep-sea-mined minerals

   U.S. firms could therefore fund and profit from foreign-flagged operations, and the U.S. would remain a market for the output.

13. **[Priority] Sec. 3, relationship to existing law.** The bill doesn't amend or repeal the Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act (30 U.S.C. 1401 et seq.), which authorizes NOAA to issue exploration licenses and commercial recovery permits. It also doesn't address mineral leasing under the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act. As a result, agencies may keep issuing authorizations, and companies will argue that the two statutes conflict. Counsel should confirm how this interacts with the pending DSHMRA applications.

14. **[Priority] Sec. 3(b), the exploration-license grandfather.** The exemption covers "mining," not just exploration, under any pre-enactment exploration license. It has:
   - no tonnage cap
   - no expiration date
   - no limit on renewals, extensions, modifications, or transfers

   A license holder could arguably conduct commercial-scale recovery indefinitely.

15. **Sec. 3(b), "an exploration license."** The bill doesn't specify who issued the license. That could let in ISA exploration contracts or licenses from foreign sponsoring states, not just NOAA licenses. It also invites a rush to obtain licenses before enactment.

16. **[Priority] Sec. 3(c), the environmental-assessment exemption.** "Environmental assessment" is undefined. The exemption requires no permit, has no volume limit, needs no agency approval, and turns entirely on the operator's self-declared purpose. Nearly any operation could be labeled "assessment," so this exemption could swallow the rule.

## Sec. 4: Registry

17. **[Priority] Sec. 4, no penalty.** Sec. 5 penalizes only violations of Sec. 3. Failing to register, failing to report, or filing false reports carries no penalty under this Act (only general statutes like 18 U.S.C. 1001 might apply).

18. **Sec. 4(b), self-certified reports.** Reports are certified only by the operator. The bill provides no independent verification, vessel tracking, observers, inspection authority, or required contents such as tonnage, location, and depth. Without that information, the 10,000-ton threshold can't be enforced.

19. **Sec. 4, scope and authority.** "Operator" is undefined. The bill doesn't say whether foreign operators or foreign-flagged vessels must register, sets no registration deadline, and gives NOAA no rulemaking authority. Reports are not required to be made public.

## Sec. 5: Penalties

20. **[Priority] Sec. 5(a) vs. Sec. 8, conflicting dates.** Civil penalties apply to violations "on or after the date of enactment," but the Act takes effect 180 days later. Defendants will argue that penalties for the gap period are invalid or unfair, and the inconsistency signals sloppy drafting that courts may resolve against enforcement.

21. **Sec. 5(a), no enforcement mechanism.** The bill doesn't say who assesses penalties, whether that happens administratively or in court, or what procedure applies. It provides no investigative or subpoena authority, no citizen suit provision, and no forfeiture of vessels or recovered minerals.

22. **Sec. 5(a), "each day on which the violation occurs."** A daily penalty doesn't fit an annual tonnage threshold. It's unclear whether a violation begins only on the day the 10,000th ton is recovered, or whether the whole year is in violation.

23. **Sec. 5(b), criminal liability tied to Sec. 2(1)(B).** Imposing up to 10 years' imprisonment for activities defined by an unstructured Secretary determination raises serious vagueness and nondelegation problems (see item 8). A court could strike down 2(1)(B), or the criminal provision, on these grounds.

## Sec. 6: International Agreement

24. **Sec. 6, "shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months."** It's ambiguous whether the deadline applies to starting negotiations or concluding them. "Seek to" creates no enforceable obligation, and there's no reporting requirement to Congress.

25. **Sec. 6, "equivalent to those in section 3."** This would export Sec. 3's weaknesses, including the grandfather and assessment exemptions, into any treaty.

## Sec. 7: Duration

26. **[Priority] Sec. 7(a) vs. 7(b), contradiction.** Sec. 7(a) says the prohibition lasts until Congress makes a scientific finding. Sec. 7(b) ends the entire Act after 10 years regardless. In practice the ban simply expires, with no finding that mining is safe.

27. **Sec. 7(a), "without serious harm."** The standard is undefined. The bill doesn't require the National Academies to produce a report or set any timeline, and a joint resolution has the same force as a regular bill, so this clause adds little.

28. **Sec. 7(b), sunset scope.** "This Act shall cease to have effect" also ends the registry and arguably wipes out pending enforcement actions, because there is no savings clause for violations that occurred before the sunset. Since the 10 years run from enactment, not from the effective date, the ban's effective life is only 9.5 years.

## Sec. 8: Effective Date

29. **[Priority] Sec. 8, 180-day delay.** This gives companies a six-month window after enactment to mine without restriction and to position themselves under the exemptions.

## Bill-Wide Gaps

30. **No severability clause.** If a court strikes down Sec. 2(1)(B) or the extraterritorial reach, a challenger can argue the whole Act falls.

31. **No general rulemaking authority, and no implementing agency is designated.** This leaves NOAA and the undefined "Secretary" without clear power to issue implementing regulations.

32. **Takings exposure.** The bill provides no compensation framework or transition mechanism. That invites Fifth Amendment takings claims from license holders and permit applicants, especially those affected by a future Sec. 2(1)(B) determination.

## Suggested Fixes to Prioritize for Markup

- Make the tonnage threshold aggregate across all vessels per operator and affiliate, or drop it.
- Narrow or sunset the Sec. 3(b) grandfather and limit it to exploration only.
- Define and require permits for Sec. 3(c) assessment activities.
- Expand "U.S. person" to cover all entity types and controlled foreign affiliates.
- Add bans on financing and imports.
- Expressly amend DSHMRA.
- Fix the Sec. 5/Sec. 8 date conflict.
- Penalize registry violations.
- Strike or rewrite the Sec. 7(b) sunset.
- Add a severability clause.

Please have counsel check the DSHMRA and OCSLA interactions in particular, since the current status of pending NOAA applications may have changed.
